purpose: Dashboard concept and original scene photography; no physical lamps depicted

prompts.concept_v1:
Use case: ui-mockup.
Create a single exceptional high-fidelity desktop dashboard design concept for "Open Keylight", an open-source studio lighting controller running directly on a lamp. This is a product interface, not a marketing landing page. A lovingly art-directed professional creative tool, quiet precision, modern editorial typography, beautifully balanced spacing and exact aligned controls. A real implementable web interface at landscape 1536x1024.

Dark graphite and near-black neutral surfaces, warm ivory text, restrained tangerine/copper accent for navigation and actions, rich saturated cobalt colour only where it represents the selected light. No muddy olive tint. Refined thin dividers and almost invisible borders, no excessive nested rounded cards. Large elegant sans typography, small monospaced numeric readings. Tasteful depth, absolutely crisp high-contrast labels.

Layout: slim left navigation rail 210px wide, top small brand "OPEN KEYLIGHT" with tiny warm circle mark. Navigation "Light" selected, "Scenes", "System", bottom "LOCAL · PRIVATE". Main wide content area. Top header small eyebrow "YOUR STUDIO", large "Storm Rim" and a small green dot "Connected"; right accessible power toggle "Light on" and small "Recording lock" control. A fine horizontal rule.
Below this: deliberate two-column lighting workspace with a generous atmospheric colour preview on left and beautiful precision controls on right. LEFT: an abstract softly illuminated cobalt circle against charcoal, almost like diffused light in air but restrained, NO physical lamp or keylight depicted. Circle is a live colour visualization, not a fake hardware knob. Small label "COLOUR OUTPUT", large hex "#245CFF", lower small RGB values "36 / 92 / 255". RIGHT: segmented "White / Colour / Effects" with Colour selected. Large "Intensity" label and "72%" numeric, long fine horizontal slider with a precise handle. "Colour" with a compact hue/saturation field and small usable swatches. Two neatly aligned controls "Smooth transition" toggle on and "Fade duration 1.2 s" slider. A subtle warm accent button "Save as scene".
Bottom: "A change of atmosphere" with four horizontal scene tiles, each an abstract photograph of softly lit surfaces in its colours, never any physical lamps: "Focus" warm ivory desk surface, "Blue hour" cobalt pool of light, "Ember" coral/amber, "Afterglow" lilac. Each image has refined legible caption outside its picture. Bottom subtle footer "Changes stay on your light."

Make this feel like a premium crafted lighting instrument someone would love to use daily. Strong hierarchy, spatial confidence, useful large controls, sensible density, artistry through colour and proportion. NO browser chrome, NO laptop frame, NO physical keylights or lighting products anywhere. No stock chart cards, no purple SaaS gradients, no decorative gibberish, no excessive glow or gratuitous illustrations. Every control is plausible and legible.
prompts.concept_v2:
Use case: ui-mockup. Refine the attached Open Keylight desktop dashboard concept into the final production design. Preserve its excellent graphite/ivory/copper palette, left navigation, professional spacing, big Storm Rim heading, practical two-column control area, and four photographic atmosphere tiles. NO physical keylight, lamp, or lighting fixture anywhere.
Targeted refinement: make the colour control itself more beautifully precise and less like a generic spectrum box. Use a large clean round hue ring with a dark central saturation/value field and an ivory selection handle, neatly balanced alongside labeled hex "#245CFF" and three compact editable numeric fields "R 36", "G 92", "B 255". Keep the intensity slider above. Keep the atmospheric blue circle on the left but make its diffusion finer and less blown out, almost velvet, with a deep dark blue center and a luminous rim. This left region is a visual preview, not a control.
Improve the type hierarchy with a slightly smaller Storm Rim title and more breathing space beneath it. Copper should be restrained on active indicator, slider fill and save button. Keep exact functional labels: "White", "Colour", "Effects", "Intensity", "72%", "Smooth transition", "Fade duration", "1.2 s", "Save as scene", "Recording lock", "Light on". 
Bottom four scene cards retain the luminous photographic table/wall imagery; captions ONLY "Focus", "Blue hour", "Ember", "Afterglow". Remove the marketing slogans under them, and remove the decorative footer sentence. Header for scenes is simply "Scenes" with small "View all" at right. Make margins, dividers, alignment and control sizes extremely intentional. No gratuitous charts, no added functionality, no giant callouts, no fake statistics. Final polished implementable interface, landscape 1536x1024, crisp legible labels.
prompts.scene_atlas: Use case: photorealistic-natural. Asset type: a four-panel scene-image atlas for an embedded studio lighting dashboard. Create a very wide 3:1 landscape raster with FOUR perfectly equal-width vertical panels edge-to-edge and no gutters or borders. Each panel is an elegant close photograph of a minimalist tabletop meeting a plaster wall, softly illuminated, subtle material grain, dramatic soft shadows. Panel 1 warm ivory sunlight, panel 2 deep luminous cobalt blue, panel 3 rich copper orange, panel 4 soft lavender violet. The four photographs should feel like four colour atmospheres in the same sophisticated quiet workspace, each with a different naturally falling light pattern. Shadows can be from unseen plants or a window; no visible equipment. Beautiful editorial photography, rich shadows, clean composition. Absolutely NO text, no labels, no logos, no physical lamps, no keylight, no monitors, no people, no furniture legs, no products. These are small scene thumbnails: simple readable masses of light and shadow, no tiny details. Final image is the four-panel atlas only.

encoding: Scene atlas resized to 1200 × 400 and encoded as WebP at quality 72 for the embedded asset budget; no creative pixel edits.
